title: C03B — Accepted Architecture Step by Step

sections.title: B. Refine the Architecture Drivers

blocks.content: A driver is a requirement, constraint, or risk that influences architecture. It explains what the system must handle and why; it does not prescribe the technical solution. We selected four drivers from C02 and the C03A investigation.

rows: BR-02 — Consultation slot exclusivity: one slot may have at most one active PENDING or CONFIRMED reservation. Sources: C02 REQ-01 — Create Reservation, REQ-02 — Check Availability, REQ-03 — Confirm Reservation, and database migration V1.
Two requests may arrive almost simultaneously. An application check alone may allow both requests to pass.
Which layer is the final authority that rejects a second active reservation for the same slot?
REQ-05 — Approve Reservation: only the teacher who owns the slot may change PENDING to CONFIRMED. Sources: C02 and the verified C03A scenarios.
The decision depends on the signed-in user role and slot ownership. Identity must come from a verified session.
Where are the actor role, slot ownership, and permitted source state checked?

REQ-04 — Cancel Reservation and transition history: a student cancels their own reservation; a teacher cancels a reservation for their slot; the change is recorded. Sources: C02 and ReservationHistory.
A state change without matching history would make it impossible to explain who changed a reservation and why.
Where are the state change and history write coordinated so one cannot be saved without the other?
In-app notification after a reservation change. Sources: the existing NotificationService and migration V11.
Reservation state and notifications are stored in the same database. A notification write failure must not leave an ambiguous partial outcome.
Where is notification creation coupled to the reservation transaction, and what is the accepted failure behavior?

blocks.content: The requirements and risks above are the drivers. ReservationService, transactions, the database index, and NotificationService are chosen solutions; they are not the drivers themselves.

sections.title: C1. Domain Model — Concepts and Relationships

blocks.content: The domain model describes reservation concepts, not technical components. This scenario uses students, teachers, consultation slots, reservations, history, and internal notifications.

Student / Teacher
  are user roles

Teacher 1 ─── 0..* ConsultationSlot
  a teacher creates and owns their consultation slots

ConsultationSlot 1 ─── 0..* Reservation
  a slot may have reservation history, but at most one active
  Reservation with status PENDING or CONFIRMED

Student 1 ─── 0..* Reservation
  the student is the consultation requester

Reservation 1 ─── 0..* ReservationHistory
  history records actions, previous/new status, actor, and note

Reservation 1 ─── 0..* Notification
  a reservation change may create an internal message for a recipient

Reservation.status:
  PENDING | CONFIRMED | CANCELLED
Key invariant: PENDING and CONFIRMED block a ConsultationSlot; CANCELLED releases it. Slot intervals use [start, end), so one slot may end exactly when the next begins.
Controller, Repository, HTTP client, and Spring are technical elements. They belong in a design class diagram, not in this domain concept model.

blocks.content: Responsibilities that share reservation state or the exclusivity invariant must be coordinated. User interface, HTTP mapping, and database access have different reasons to change, so they are separated from business-rule decisions.

sections.title: D. One Main Decision Question

blocks.content: The decision question connects the most important drivers to the design. It must have at least two realistic architectural answers.
Where should the authoritative reservation lifecycle decision be owned so that actor authorization, reservation state, history, internal notification, and database exclusivity remain consistent?

items: It follows from BR-02 — Consultation slot exclusivity, REQ-05 — Approve Reservation, REQ-04 — Cancel Reservation, and the requirement to preserve history.
It affects backend structure, the transaction boundary, security checks, and the location of database constraints.
It can be answered by application-service orchestration or a database-owned workflow.

sections.title: E1. Two Materially Different Alternatives

blocks.content: Both alternatives answer the same question. They differ in which part of the system owns the rules and coordinates a reservation change.

rows: A — Transactional application service.

One backend use case loads the reservation, verifies the actor and rules, changes the domain object, writes history, and creates an internal notification in one database transaction. The database unique index remains the final slot guard.
The application service owns the decision and order of steps; the domain object changes state; the database enforces data constraints.
B — Database-owned workflow.

A database function or procedure decides the state transition and writes the reservation, history, and notification in the database. The backend passes the request and maps the result to an HTTP response.
The database layer owns the main workflow; the application layer supplies parameters and maps errors.

blocks.content: A controller or frontend could also orchestrate the steps, but we did not select it as a full alternative: it would scatter rules, and a client cannot be authoritative for authorization or concurrency.

sections.title: E2. Compare Alternatives Against the Drivers

blocks.content: The criteria below come directly from the drivers in section B. The table gives concrete consequences rather than unexplained scores.

rows: BR-02 — Slot exclusivity and concurrency.
The application check explains ordinary conflicts; the one_active_reservation_per_slot unique index rejects a second write under concurrency and the service returns HTTP 409.
A database procedure can check close to the data; a unique index or equivalent database constraint is still required.
REQ-05 — Approval authorization and decision.
The service receives AuthenticatedUser from the verified session and checks the active role and slot ownership before the transition.
The database workflow must receive a trustworthy actor identifier. A database procedure alone cannot verify the application bearer session.
REQ-04 — State and audit history.
One service method coordinates the domain transition and ReservationHistory write in a transaction.
Transition and history can be atomic in the database, but rules and their rationale become hidden in procedures or triggers.
Internal notification and failure boundary.
NotificationService writes the notification synchronously to the same database; a failure in the transaction rolls back the operation.
The database can also insert the notification, but that adds more application workflow rules to the database.
Rule changes and operational complexity.
The Spring Boot monolith has one readable place for the rules; this matches current deployment.
Business workflow in SQL and database error mapping must be maintained; that adds complexity for this monolith.

sections.title: E3. Walk Both Alternatives Through the Same Scenario

blocks.content: We use the C02 and C03A scenario: a teacher approves a pending reservation. Complication: another request for the same slot arrives at the same time. PENDING already blocks the slot, so the second request must not create another active reservation.

rows: 1. Approval starts.
The service loads the reservation and verifies the signed-in teacher, slot ownership, and PENDING state.
The backend passes the reservation ID and the identity verified by the application security layer; the database loads the state and owner.
2. A second request arrives concurrently.
Create checks for an active reservation; even if application checks overlap, the unique index rejects the second active write.
The database workflow and unique constraint reject the second active reservation in the database.
3. Approval.
The domain object changes from PENDING to CONFIRMED. The slot remains continuously blocked because both states are active.
The procedure changes PENDING to CONFIRMED in the database; the constraint must remain valid throughout the transition.
4. History and notification.
The service writes history and the internal notification in the same transaction as the state change.
The database workflow must write history and notification in the same transaction or it can leave a partial outcome.
5. Response.
Approval returns a confirmed reservation; the second create request returns HTTP 409.
The backend maps the procedure result or database error to the matching HTTP response.

blocks.content: Both alternatives can preserve the invariant if they use the database constraint correctly. We selected A because the rules remain readable in the application and match the existing Spring Boot monolith.

sections.title: F. ADR-01 — Reservation Lifecycle Ownership Decision

blocks.content:
Context:
  A reservation transitions from PENDING to CONFIRMED or CANCELLED.
  A change must verify the actor, preserve slot exclusivity,
  write history, and create an internal notification.

Drivers:
  BR-02 — Slot exclusivity; REQ-05 — approval by slot owner;
  REQ-04 — authorized cancellation and history; internal notification.

Alternatives considered:
  A — transactional application service coordinates rules and writes.
  B — database function/procedure owns the main workflow.

Decision:
  Accept option A. ReservationService coordinates create/approve/cancel
  in a transaction; Reservation performs the domain transition; PostgreSQL
  enforces one active reservation per slot.

Reason:
  This fits the Spring Boot monolith and keeps business rules in readable,
  testable application code. The database remains authoritative for integrity
  and concurrency.

Accepted downside:
  Internal notifications are written synchronously in the same database
  transaction. There is no external delivery, queue, or automatic retry.

Reconsider this decision when:
  notifications use an external delivery service or reliable retries are
  required, or when the database invariant is insufficient for a new
  operational model.

sections.title: H1. Design Sequence — Approving a Reservation

blocks.content: C03A mapped reservation approval, so this is the main H1 scenario. It shows the target architecture, significant calls, security checks, state change, and an error branch.

Teacher → TeacherPage:
  selects a PENDING request and chooses Approve

  approveReservation(token, reservationId)

API client → ReservationController:
  POST /api/reservations/{reservationId}/approve

BearerTokenFilter → AuthService:
  verifies bearer token and places AuthenticatedUser in SecurityContext

ReservationController → ReservationService:
  approve(reservationId, AuthenticatedUser, request)

ReservationService → ReservationRepository:
  loads reservation

ReservationService:
  verifies signed-in actor, active TEACHER role,
  slot ownership, and PENDING state

alt verification fails
  ReservationService → Controller:
    ApiException 401 / 403 / 404 / 409
